design_rationale: The study explicitly reports generation of a random allocation sequence and assignment of 358 enrolled students to an experimental or waitlisted control group.

domain_judgments.rationale: A random allocation sequence and separate research assistants for enrollment and assignment were reported, and measured baseline characteristics were broadly similar, but the sequence-generation method and allocation-concealment safeguards were not described.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The first author (HSYM) generated a random allocation sequence table. Two research assistants were responsible for then enrolling and assigning the participants to either the experimental group or a waitlisted control group.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily knew whether they received face-to-face training, contamination was possible within the single institution, and 14 intervention participants did not complete training/post-test, although the analysis was reported as intention-to-treat.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All the nursing students were recruited from a single tertiary institution, so study contamination may have occurred, although the students were also instructed to avoid disclosing any study information to their peers.

domain_judgments.rationale: Attrition was modest but differential at follow-up, and missing outcomes were replaced using last observation carried forward without evidence that missingness could not bias the results.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The missing data for every outcome measure were imputed by using the last-observationcarried-forward method.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcomes were measured consistently with generally validated self-report questionnaires, but participants were unblinded and most outcomes—knowledge, attitudes, confidence, helping behavior, and wellbeing—were susceptible to intervention-related expectancy and social-desirability effects, making differential measurement error likely.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The outcomes were measured in terms of local relevance and application, according to the participants’ self-completed responses to two well-validated questionnaires: the Mental Health Literacy Scale (Chinese version) and the Chinese Health Questionnaire (CHQ).

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, while numerous outcomes, time points, scenarios, and post hoc comparisons allowed analytic and reporting flexibility.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A repeated-measures analysis of variance with Greenhouse-Geisser correction was used to investigate the effectiveness of MHFA training.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high because the unblinded behavioral intervention relied predominantly on participant-reported outcomes that could readily be influenced by knowledge of assignment. Additional concerns arise from incompletely described allocation concealment, possible contamination, last-observation-carried-forward imputation, and lack of reported preregistration.

design_rationale: This was an explicitly cluster-randomized trial: schools were paired and one school in each pair was assigned using random integers generated by Random.org.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although sequence generation was random, allocation was disclosed before baseline measurement and two schools changed their assigned timing after randomization, with the primary analysis then excluding those nonadherent clusters; baseline imbalances were also observed.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Schools were told about the allocation before their teachers completed the pre-test questionnaire... it was agreed to swap the allocation for these two schools (one from intervention to control and the other from control to intervention), resulting in 14, rather than 16 schools receiving the intervention as randomized.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and schools knew allocation, two randomized schools did not follow their assignments, and the primary analysis excluded those clusters rather than maintaining assignment in an intention-to-treat analysis, creating potential bias from deviations related to context and scheduling.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All participants who completed a pre-test questionnaire and were at one of the 14 schools that adhered to randomization were included in the analysis. However, a supplementary analysis was also carried out which included the 2 additional schools that did not adhere.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome attrition was substantial (22–28% among teachers and 24% among students), and the mixed-model analysis was unbiased only under an unverified missing-at-random assumption, with no reported sensitivity analysis establishing robustness to informative missingness.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Twenty-two percent of teachers did not complete the post-test questionnaire and 28% the follow-up questionnaire. In relation to the students, 24% did not complete the follow-up questionnaire.

domain_judgments.rationale: The primary outcome and many secondary outcomes were self-completed by unblinded teachers, and intervention knowledge could plausibly influence responses, while allocation was known before baseline assessment; thus differential measurement bias is plausible despite identical questionnaires across groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Blinding of participants was not possible. Post-test and follow-up questionnaires were self-completed by teachers who knew whether they had completed the training or not.

domain_judgments.rationale: Despite trial registration and a stated primary outcome, numerous outcomes, individual stigma items, time points, and supplementary analyses were available, the stigma scale was changed to item-level analysis after inspecting the data, and the authors acknowledged extensive multiplicity without reported multiplicity control or a prespecified analysis plan.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: These items were intended to be analyzed as scales based on a previous principal components analysis. However, because the principal components could not be replicated in the teacher data, the responses to these questions were analyzed as individual items.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high. The main drivers are post-randomization departures from assignment coupled with exclusion of two nonadherent schools from the primary analysis, unblinded self-reported outcomes, and substantial scope for selective reporting across many outcomes and analyses; appreciable attrition adds further concern.

design_rationale: This was an individually randomized, three-arm parallel trial using a computerized random-number generator to assign participants to the e-learning CD, printed manual, or waiting-list control.

domain_judgments.rationale: The allocation sequence was generated randomly, concealed until after baseline assessment, and implemented through separation of enrolment and sequence generation; reported baseline differences do not suggest a clear randomization failure.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A computerized random number generator (Random Integers option in Random.org) was used to carry out a simple randomization procedure... The allocation sequence was concealed from J.F. until it was time to advise participants of their random assignment... after baseline data was collected.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants could not be blinded and adherence differed or was incompletely observed, but the intended educational materials and pacing contacts were standardized and analyses followed intention-to-treat principles.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Blinding of participants was not possible... An intention-to-treat approach was used, with all participants included in the analyses.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome attrition was modest but reached 13% at follow-up and differed by group; maximum-likelihood mixed models are valid under a missing-at-random assumption, but evidence establishing that missingness was unrelated to outcomes was limited.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Nine per cent of participants did not complete the post-test questionnaire and 13% the follow-up questionnaire... there were differences in sample retention across groups, with the waiting list group having the best retention and the CD group the worst.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcomes were assessed consistently with established questionnaires, but they were participant-reported and participants knew their assignment, so expectations or social desirability could have influenced stigma, confidence, helping-behavior, and mental-health reports.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Blinding of participants was not possible... The effects of the interventions were evaluated using online questionnaires pre- and post-training and at 6-months follow up.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered and hypotheses were stated, but numerous outcomes, dichotomized operationalizations, time points, contrasts, and a labeled secondary analysis created scope for selective reporting, with no protocol or prespecified analysis plan provided in the text to resolve this concern.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The trial has been registered with the Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ACTRN12608000188336)... However, a secondary analysis of the ‘ days of out of role ’ questions... showed that the CD group had significantly greater reduction.

overall_summary: The randomization process was robust, and no domain was judged high risk. Some concerns remain because participants were unblinded for subjective self-reported outcomes, follow-up data were differentially missing across groups, and the many outcomes and analyses leave some potential for selective reporting.

design_rationale: Participants who consented and completed baseline questionnaires were explicitly allocated using the Random Integers option at random.org to immediate MHFA training or a six-month waiting-list control.

domain_judgments.rationale: The allocation sequence was generated electronically by a researcher using an anonymized participant list, and the closely balanced baseline characteristics provide no indication of a randomization failure.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Each participant was given a specific ID-number on the list, which was then sent to one of the researchers (BS) who performed the randomization procedure by using the Random Integers option at the http://random.org website [29]. The participants where anonymous to the researchers.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily knew whether they received immediate training or were wait-listed, and although intention-to-treat analysis was used and all intervention participants reportedly completed the course, the report gives limited information about deviations or contamination arising from the unblinded behavioral intervention.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Intention to treat analyses were performed in the RCT.

domain_judgments.rationale: About 32% of each randomized group lacked six-month questionnaires, and multiple imputation was appropriate but cannot eliminate concern because reasons for missingness and sensitivity to the imputation assumptions were not adequately established.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: At the six month follow up 64 participants in the experimental group and 65 in the control group had not completed the questionnaires.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcomes were measured identically across groups using established questionnaires, but they were self-reported by participants aware of treatment assignment, so reporting of subjective helping behavior, confidence, and attitudes could have been influenced by the intervention.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The same self – report questionnaires as in the Australian studies have been used [8,9].

domain_judgments.rationale: The report identifies primary and secondary outcomes but provides no prospective trial registration or prespecified analysis plan, and numerous outcome measures and analyses create scope for selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The primary outcome is whether individuals trained in MHFA compared to waiting – list controls improved their readiness to provide actual help to people with mental disorders. Secondary outcomes are if the training lead to more: 1. knowledge about mental disorders and their treatment, 2. knowledge about how to behave and act when with a person with a mental disorder, 3. selfconfidence in helping a person with a mental disorder, 4. positive attitudes towards people with mental disorders.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is judged some concerns. Randomization was adequate, but concerns remain because the behavioral intervention and subjective outcomes were unblinded, roughly one-third of six-month outcomes were missing and imputed, and no prospective protocol or prespecified analysis plan was reported.

design_rationale: The study explicitly reports participant allocation using an independent researcher’s computer-generated concealed randomization sequence with variable block sizes.

domain_judgments.rationale: The allocation sequence was computer-generated by an independent researcher, concealed, and the reported baseline characteristics showed no important group imbalances.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: An independent researcher provided the randomization by a computer-generated concealed randomization sequence with variable block size.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although intention-to-treat analysis was used, participants and instructors were unblinded and coworkers shared workplaces across groups, creating a reported risk of contamination that could dilute intervention effects.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The trial also implied a risk of contamination between the two groups. The participants were often sharing workplace cross-groups, and experiences and knowledge gained at the training course could have been subject to exchange between the groups in unrelated contexts.

domain_judgments.rationale: Six-month outcome data were missing for a large and different proportion of participants across groups (40% versus 29%), and multiple imputation used only age and gender under an unverified missing-at-random assumption, so outcome-dependent missingness could materially bias results.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: At 6 months follow-up 117 (40 %) participants in the intervention group and 80 (29 %) in the control group had not completed the questionnaire.

domain_judgments.rationale: The primary confidence outcomes were subjective self-reports from participants who necessarily knew whether they had received training, making intervention-related reporting bias likely despite identical measurement procedures across groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: However, neither the participants, the assessors (the trial being a self-report study) nor the instructors were blinded.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was registered only after recruitment/analysis timing is unclear, the full prespecified analysis plan was not presented, and numerous outcome items and analyses were available, leaving scope for selective reporting even though a protocol could be requested.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The protocol was registered at https://clinicaltrials.gov on the 25th of April 2015, identifier NCT02334020.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by substantial differential attrition handled through imputation under an uncertain missing-at-random assumption and by subjective self-reported primary outcomes from unblinded participants. Possible contamination and uncertainty about selective reporting add further concerns.
